steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on training neural networks with logical constraints without shortcut satisfaction. Explain the shortcut satisfaction problem and the joint-training incompatibility of existing logic-to-loss methods, and introduce our dual-variable logic encoding, the variational framework, and our contributions.

steps.text:

- Problem 1: shortcut satisfaction (Figure 1 example)
- Our fix: dual variables to model how a constraint is satisfied

- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - renewed interest: DNNs + symbolic knowledge (logical constraints/formulas)
  - typical: translate constraint into differentiable loss, add as penalty to training loss
  - benefits: better performance, interpretability by regulating model behavior
- Shortcut satisfaction
  - model overfits to a particular (easy) satisfying assignment
  - not all satisfying assignments are the truth; different inputs need different assignments
  - Figure 1: constraint P\rightarrow Q, holds when (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) or (P,Q)=(\textbf{F},\textbf{F})/(\textbf{F},\textbf{T})
  - existing approaches assign F to P for all inputs, even when meaning is (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) for some inputs (class ‘6’)
- Dual variables
  - consider how a constraint is satisfied; distinguish satisfying assignments per input
  - challenge: no direct supervision of how, only truth value
  - insight: harder problem -> more room to reconcile logic and data; better accuracy and logic satisfaction
  - dual variable per operand of logical connectives in CNF; with softened truth values -> working interpretation of satisfaction
  - example: CNF \neg P\vee Q, variables \tau_{1}, \tau_{2} weighting softened truth values of \neg P and Q
  - blue dashed lines in right part of Figure 1 (P-/Q-Satisfaction subfigures): dual variables converge to intended weights for class ‘6’
- Convex combinations
  - conjunction/disjunction -> convex combinations of individual losses
  - training robustness; monotonicity w.r.t. logical entailment (smaller loss, higher satisfaction)
  - most existing translations only guarantee full satisfaction at zero loss; full satisfaction virtually infeasible -> unreliable training
- Incompatibility
  - logic loss as penalty in multi-objective learning; depends on weight selection; suffers when objectives compete
  - ours: extra random variable for satisfaction degree; distributional loss compatible with original loss under variational framework
  - joint optimization as a game; stochastic gradient descent ascent; converges to superset of local Nash equilibria
- Contributions
  1. logic encoding considering how constraints are satisfied, avoiding shortcut satisfaction
  2. variational framework, joint compatible training, guaranteed convergence
  3. extensive evaluations: accuracy and constraint satisfaction

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There has been renewed interest in giving deep neural networks (DNNs) symbolic knowledge such as logical constraints/formulas. Usually, existing work first translates the given logical constraint into a differentiable loss function and then adds it as a penalty term to the original training loss of the DNN. The benefits of doing this are well-demonstrated: it improves the performance, and it also improves interpretability by regulating the model behavior so it satisfies particular logical constraints.

Despite this progress, existing approaches tend to have the shortcut satisfaction problem, where the model overfits to a particular (easy) satisfying assignment of the given logical constraint. But not all satisfying assignments are the truth, and different inputs may need different assignments to satisfy the same constraint. Figure 1 gives an illustrative example. The example considers a logical constraint P\rightarrow Q, which holds when (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) or (P,Q)=(\textbf{F},\textbf{F})/(\textbf{F},\textbf{T}). But we observe that existing approaches tend to just satisfy the constraint by assigning F to P for all inputs, even when the real meaning of the logic constraint is arguably (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) for some inputs (e.g., class ‘6’ in the example).

To escape shortcut satisfaction, we propose to consider how a logical constraint is satisfied, by distinguishing between different satisfying assignments of the constraint for different inputs. The challenge is that there is no direct supervision of how a constraint is satisfied, only its truth value. Our insight is that by addressing this “harder” problem we make more room for reconciling logic information and training data, and we get better model performance and logic satisfaction at the same time. So when we translate a logical constraint into a loss function, we introduce a dual variable for each operand of the logical connectives in the conjunctive normal form (CNF) of the logical constraint. Together with the softened truth values for logical variables, the dual variables give a working interpretation of how the logical constraint is satisfied. In the example in Figure 1, for the satisfaction of P\rightarrow Q we consider its CNF \neg P\vee Q and introduce two variables \tau_{1} and \tau_{2} that indicate the weights of the softened truth values of \neg P and Q. The blue dashed lines in the right part of Figure 1 (the P -Satisfaction and Q -Satisfaction subfigures) show that the dual variables gradually converge to the intended weights for class ‘6’.

- Convex combinations
  - conjunction/disjunction -> convex combinations of individual losses
  - training robustness; monotonicity w.r.t. logical entailment (smaller loss, higher satisfaction)
  - most existing translations only guarantee full satisfaction at zero loss; full satisfaction virtually infeasible -> unreliable training
- Incompatibility
  - logic loss as penalty in multi-objective learning; depends on weight selection; suffers when objectives compete
  - ours: extra random variable for satisfaction degree; distributional loss compatible with original loss under variational framework
  - joint optimization as a game; stochastic gradient descent ascent; converges to superset of local Nash equilibria
- Contributions
  1. logic encoding considering how constraints are satisfied, avoiding shortcut satisfaction
  2. variational framework, joint compatible training, guaranteed convergence
  3. extensive evaluations: accuracy and constraint satisfaction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There has been renewed interest in giving deep neural networks (DNNs) symbolic knowledge such as logical constraints/formulas. Usually, existing work first translates the given logical constraint into a differentiable loss function and then adds it as a penalty term to the original training loss of the DNN. The benefits of doing this are well-demonstrated: it improves the performance, and it also improves interpretability by regulating the model behavior so it satisfies particular logical constraints.

Despite this progress, existing approaches tend to have the shortcut satisfaction problem, where the model overfits to a particular (easy) satisfying assignment of the given logical constraint. But not all satisfying assignments are the truth, and different inputs may need different assignments to satisfy the same constraint. Figure 1 gives an illustrative example. The example considers a logical constraint P\rightarrow Q, which holds when (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) or (P,Q)=(\textbf{F},\textbf{F})/(\textbf{F},\textbf{T}). But we observe that existing approaches tend to just satisfy the constraint by assigning F to P for all inputs, even when the real meaning of the logic constraint is arguably (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) for some inputs (e.g., class ‘6’ in the example).

To escape shortcut satisfaction, we propose to consider how a logical constraint is satisfied, by distinguishing between different satisfying assignments of the constraint for different inputs. The challenge is that there is no direct supervision of how a constraint is satisfied, only its truth value. Our insight is that by addressing this “harder” problem we make more room for reconciling logic information and training data, and we get better model performance and logic satisfaction at the same time. So when we translate a logical constraint into a loss function, we introduce a dual variable for each operand of the logical connectives in the conjunctive normal form (CNF) of the logical constraint. Together with the softened truth values for logical variables, the dual variables give a working interpretation of how the logical constraint is satisfied. In the example in Figure 1, for the satisfaction of P\rightarrow Q we consider its CNF \neg P\vee Q and introduce two variables \tau_{1} and \tau_{2} that indicate the weights of the softened truth values of \neg P and Q. The blue dashed lines in the right part of Figure 1 (the P -Satisfaction and Q -Satisfaction subfigures) show that the dual variables gradually converge to the intended weights for class ‘6’.

Using the dual variables, we then turn logical conjunction and disjunction into convex combinations of individual loss functions. This improves training robustness and also ensures monotonicity with respect to logical entailment, which means the smaller the loss, the higher the satisfaction. Most existing logic to loss translations do not have this property, they only ensure that the logical constraint is fully satisfied when the loss is zero, but in practice it is virtually infeasible to fully satisfy the logical constraint, so the training process towards constraint satisfaction is unreliable.

Another limitation of existing approaches is incompatibility during joint training. Existing work mostly treats the translated logic loss as a penalty in a multi-objective learning framework, and how well this works depends strongly on the weight selection for each objective, and it may suffer when the objectives compete. Instead, we introduce an additional random variable for the logical constraint that indicates its satisfaction degree, and formulate it as a distributional loss which is compatible with the original training loss of the neural network under a variational framework. We cast the joint optimization of prediction accuracy and constraint satisfaction as a game and propose a stochastic gradient descent ascent algorithm to solve it. Theoretical results show that the algorithm converges to a superset of local Nash equilibria, so it largely settles the incompatibility problem.

In summary, the main contributions of this paper are: 1) a new logic encoding method that translates logical constraints to loss functions while considering how the constraints are satisfied, in particular to avoid shortcut satisfaction; 2) a variational framework that trains both the translated logic loss and the original training loss jointly and compatibly, with theoretically guaranteed convergence; 3) extensive empirical evaluations on various tasks that show superior performance in both accuracy and constraint satisfaction, confirming that the proposed approach works.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
There has been renewed interest in equipping deep neural networks (DNNs) with symbolic knowledge such as logical constraints/formulas [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. Typically, existing work first translates the given logical constraint into a differentiable loss function, and then incorporates it as a penalty term in the original training loss of the DNN. The benefits of this integration have been well-demonstrated: it not only improves performance, but also enhances interpretability by regulating the model behavior to satisfy particular logical constraints.

Despite the encouraging progress, existing approaches tend to suffer from the shortcut satisfaction problem, i.e., the model overfits to a particular (easy) satisfying assignment of the given logical constraint. However, not all satisfying assignments are the truth, and different inputs may require different assignments to satisfy the same constraint. An illustrative example is given in Figure 1. The example considers a logical constraint P\rightarrow Q, which holds when (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) or (P,Q)=(\textbf{F},\textbf{F})/(\textbf{F},\textbf{T}). However, we observe that existing approaches tend to simply satisfy the constraint by assigning F to P for all inputs, even when the real meaning of the logic constraint is arguably (P,Q)=(\textbf{T},\textbf{T}) for certain inputs (e.g., class ‘6’ in the example).

To escape the trap of shortcut satisfaction, we propose to consider how a logical constraint is satisfied by distinguishing between different satisfying assignments of the constraint for different inputs. The challenge here is the lack of direct supervision on how a constraint is satisfied, other than its truth value. However, our insight is that by addressing this “harder” problem, we can make more room for the conciliation between logic information and training data, and achieve better model performance and logic satisfaction at the same time. To this end, when translating a logical constraint into a loss function, we introduce a dual variable for each operand of the logical connectives in the conjunctive normal form (CNF) of the logical constraint. The dual variables, together with the softened truth values for logical variables, provide a working interpretation for the satisfaction of the logical constraint. Take the example in Figure 1: for the satisfaction of P\rightarrow Q, we consider its CNF \neg P\vee Q and introduce two variables \tau_{1} and \tau_{2} to indicate the weights of the softened truth values of \neg P and Q, respectively. The blue dashed lines in the right part of Figure 1 (the P -Satisfaction and Q -Satisfaction subfigures) indicate that the dual variables gradually converge to the intended weights for class ‘6’.

Based on the dual variables, we then convert logical conjunction and disjunction into convex combinations of individual loss functions, which not only improves training robustness but also ensures monotonicity with respect to logical entailment, i.e., the smaller the loss, the higher the satisfaction. Note that most existing logic-to-loss translations do not enjoy this property and only ensure that the logical constraint is fully satisfied when the loss is zero; however, it is virtually infeasible to fully satisfy the logical constraint in practice, which makes the training process towards constraint satisfaction unreliable.

Another limitation of existing approaches lies in incompatibility during joint training. Existing work mainly treats the translated logic loss as a penalty under a multi-objective learning framework, whose effectiveness strongly relies on the weight selection of each objective, and which may suffer when the objectives compete [8,9]. In contrast, we introduce an additional random variable for the logical constraint to indicate its satisfaction degree, and formulate it as a distributional loss that is compatible with the neural network’s original training loss under a variational framework. We cast the joint optimization of prediction accuracy and constraint satisfaction as a game and propose a stochastic gradient descent ascent algorithm to solve it. Theoretical results show that the algorithm converges to a superset of local Nash equilibria, and thus settles the incompatibility problem to a large extent.

In summary, this paper makes the following main contributions: 1) a new logic encoding method that translates logical constraints to loss functions, considering how the constraints are satisfied, in particular to avoid shortcut satisfaction; 2) a variational framework that jointly and compatibly trains both the translated logic loss and the original training loss with theoretically guaranteed convergence; 3) extensive empirical evaluations on various tasks demonstrating superior performance in both accuracy and constraint satisfaction, confirming the efficacy of the proposed approach.
